UNIFORM VOIDABLE TRANSACTIONS ACT — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jane Doe or Acme LLC · John Smith or Acme Supplies Inc.

UNIFORM VOIDABLE TRANSACTIONS ACT INFORMATION SHEET — PURPOSE AND SCOPE
This information sheet relates to a transfer of property, or an obligation incurred, by Jane Doe or Acme LLC that John Smith or Acme Supplies Inc. believes may be a "voidable transaction" affecting property described as the real property at 123 Main St., or the transfer of business assets on [date]. It describes California's Uniform Voidable Transactions Act (Civil Code section 3439 et seq.), a statute that lets a creditor ask a court to void — or obtain other relief against — certain transfers a debtor made, or obligations a debtor incurred, that hindered, delayed, or defrauded the creditor, or that left the debtor without enough assets or ability to pay its debts. The statute was enacted under that name effective January 1, 2016; before that date the same chapter was known as the Uniform Fraudulent Transfer Act, and California courts and other sources may still refer to it by that earlier name when discussing older transfers or older case law. This information sheet does not itself void, ratify, or otherwise determine the legal effect of any transfer involving Jane Doe or Acme LLC or John Smith or Acme Supplies Inc., does not determine whether any particular transfer was made with the intent or under the financial circumstances the statute describes, and does not evaluate the merits of any specific claim. Whether a particular transfer or obligation is voidable under this statute is a determination made by a court applying the statute to the facts of a specific case.

KEY TERMS: "TRANSFER," "CREDITOR," "DEBTOR," AND "ASSET"
The Uniform Voidable Transactions Act defines several terms broadly. A "transfer" is every mode, direct or indirect, absolute or conditional, voluntary or involuntary, of disposing of or parting with an asset or an interest in an asset — the statute expressly includes payment of money, a release, a lease, a license, and the creation of a lien or other encumbrance within that definition, so the statute reaches far more than an outright sale or gift of property. A "creditor" is a person that has a "claim" (a right to payment, whether or not that right has been reduced to judgment, is liquidated, is fixed, is contingent, or is disputed), and a "debtor" is a person liable on a claim; a creditor need not already hold a judgment, or even an undisputed claim, to be a creditor under the statute. "Asset" means property of a debtor, but the statute excludes from "asset" property already encumbered by a valid lien, property that is generally exempt from creditors under nonbankruptcy law, and certain tenancy-by-the-entireties interests not subject to a single tenant's individual creditors.

  — Cal. Civ. Code § 3439.01(m), Uniform Voidable Transactions Act, definition of "transfer" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=3439.01.)
  "“Creditor” means a person that has a claim, and includes an assignee of a general assignment for the benefit of creditors, as defined in Section 493.010 of the Code of Civil Procedure, of a debtor.(d) “Debt” means liability on a claim.(e) “Debtor” means a person that is liable on a claim."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 3439.01(c)-(e), Uniform Voidable Transactions Act, definitions of "creditor," "debt," and "debtor" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=3439.01.)
  "“Asset” means property of a debtor, but the term does not include the following:(1) Property to the extent it is encumbered by a valid lien.(2) Property to the extent it is generally exempt under nonbankruptcy law.(3) An interest in property held in tenancy by the entireties to the extent it is not subject to process by a creditor holding a claim against only one tenant."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 3439.01(a), Uniform Voidable Transactions Act, definition of "asset" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=3439.01.)

"Insolvent" is a separate, substantive term defined in a different section (Civil Code section 3439.02) and is addressed in its own clause below rather than here.

THE STATUTORY DEFINITION OF "INSOLVENT"
The Uniform Voidable Transactions Act defines "insolvent" as a balance-sheet test: a debtor is insolvent if, at a fair valuation, the sum of the debtor's debts is greater than the sum of the debtor's assets. Separately, the statute creates a presumption of insolvency for a debtor that is generally not paying its debts as they become due, other than as a result of a bona fide dispute; once that presumption applies, it shifts the burden to the party against whom the presumption is directed to prove that it is more probable than not that the debtor was not insolvent. The statute also refines what counts as an "asset" or a "debt" for this insolvency calculation: property that has been transferred, concealed, or removed with intent to hinder, delay, or defraud creditors, or transferred in a manner making the transfer voidable under the statute, is excluded from the debtor's assets for this test, and an obligation is excluded from the debtor's debts to the extent it is secured by a valid lien on property of the debtor that is not itself counted as an asset.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]

The presumption imposes on the party against which the presumption is directed the burden of proving that the nonexistence of insolvency is more probable than its existence."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 3439.02(a)-(b), Uniform Voidable Transactions Act, definition of insolvency and presumption (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=3439.02.)

ACTUAL INTENT TO HINDER, DELAY, OR DEFRAUD
Under the Uniform Voidable Transactions Act, a transfer made, or an obligation incurred, by a debtor is voidable as to a creditor if the debtor made the transfer or incurred the obligation with actual intent to hinder, delay, or defraud any creditor of the debtor. This ground for voidability is available to a creditor regardless of whether that creditor's claim against the debtor arose before or after the transfer was made or the obligation was incurred — a creditor whose claim did not yet exist at the time of the transfer can still invoke this provision. A creditor asserting this claim for relief has the burden of proving the elements of the claim by a preponderance of the evidence; the statute does not require clear and convincing evidence or any higher standard.

  — Cal. Civ. Code § 3439.04(a) & (a)(1), Uniform Voidable Transactions Act, actual-intent voidability ground (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=3439.04.)
  "A creditor making a claim for relief under subdivision (a) has the burden of proving the elements of the claim for relief by a preponderance of the evidence."

It does not address the separate, additional constructive-fraud grounds for voidability found in the same subdivision, paragraph (2) of section 3439.04(a) (covered in a separate clause below), and it does not determine whether any specific debtor acted with the actual intent this provision describes with respect to any specific transfer.

"BADGES OF FRAUD" — FACTORS BEARING ON ACTUAL INTENT
The statute lists eleven specific factors — commonly called "badges of fraud" — that may be considered, among other factors, in determining whether a debtor acted with the actual intent to hinder, delay, or defraud a creditor: whether the transfer or obligation was to an insider; whether the debtor retained possession or control of the transferred property after the transfer; whether the transfer or obligation was disclosed or concealed; whether the debtor had been sued or threatened with suit before the transfer or obligation; whether the transfer was of substantially all of the debtor's assets; whether the debtor absconded; whether the debtor removed or concealed assets; whether the consideration the debtor received was reasonably equivalent to the value of the asset transferred or the amount of the obligation incurred; whether the debtor was insolvent or became insolvent shortly after the transfer or obligation; whether the transfer occurred shortly before or after the debtor incurred a substantial debt; and whether the debtor transferred the business's essential assets to a lienor that then transferred them to an insider of the debtor. The statute frames this as a non-exclusive list — a court may give consideration to "any or all" of these factors "among other factors," so no single factor is required and no fixed number of factors must be present.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "In determining actual intent under paragraph (1) of subdivision (a), consideration may be given, among other factors, to any or all of the following:(1) Whether the transfer or obligation was to an insider.(2) Whether the debtor retained possession or control of the property transferred after the transfer.(3) Whether the transfer or obligation was disclosed or concealed.(4) Whether before the transfer was made or obligation was incurred, the debtor had been sued or threatened with suit.(5) Whether the transfer was of substantially all the debtor’s assets.(6) Whether the debtor absconded.(7) Whether the debtor removed or concealed assets.(8) Whether the value of the consideration received by the debtor was reasonably equivalent to the value of the asset transferred or the amount of the obligation incurred.(9) Whether the debtor was insolvent or became insolvent shortly after the transfer was made or the obligation was incurred.(10) Whether the transfer occurred shortly before or shortly after a substantial debt was incurred.(11) Whether the debtor transferred the essential assets of the business to a lienor that transferred the assets to an insider of the debtor."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 3439.04(b), Uniform Voidable Transactions Act, badges-of-fraud factors (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=3439.04.)

This clause does not evaluate whether any of these factors is present with respect to any specific transfer involving any particular debtor, and satisfying one or more of these factors does not, by itself, establish actual intent to hinder, delay, or defraud under the statute.

CONSTRUCTIVE FRAUD — TRANSFERS VOIDABLE WITHOUT PROOF OF INTENT
Separate from actual intent, the statute lets a creditor void a transfer or obligation based purely on the debtor's objective financial circumstances, with no need to prove the debtor's state of mind. One provision, available to any creditor regardless of whether the creditor's claim arose before or after the transfer, makes a transfer or obligation voidable if the debtor did not receive a reasonably equivalent value in exchange, and the debtor either was engaged in or about to engage in a business or transaction for which the debtor's remaining assets were unreasonably small in relation to that business or transaction, or intended to incur, or believed or reasonably should have believed the debtor would incur, debts beyond the debtor's ability to pay them as they became due. A second, narrower provision applies only to a creditor whose claim arose before the transfer was made or the obligation was incurred: it makes the transfer or obligation voidable if the debtor did not receive a reasonably equivalent value in exchange and the debtor either was already insolvent at that time or became insolvent as a result of the transfer or obligation. In both provisions, the creditor bears the burden of proving the elements of the claim for relief by a preponderance of the evidence.

TIME LIMITS: FOUR-YEAR PERIODS AND A SEVEN-YEAR OUTER LIMIT
The statute extinguishes a cause of action under the Uniform Voidable Transactions Act unless the creditor brings an action, or makes a levy, within specific time limits, and those limits differ by which ground for voidability is invoked. For an actual-intent claim, the action must be brought no later than four years after the transfer was made or the obligation was incurred, or, if later, no later than one year after the transfer or obligation was or reasonably could have been discovered by the claimant. For either constructive-fraud claim, the action must be brought no later than four years after the transfer was made or the obligation was incurred, with no discovery-based extension. Separately, and regardless of which of these grounds applies or when the transfer or obligation was or could have been discovered, the statute imposes an absolute seven-year outer limit: a cause of action under the statute is extinguished if no action is brought and no levy is made within seven years after the transfer was made or the obligation was incurred, notwithstanding any other provision of law.

REMEDIES AVAILABLE TO A CREDITOR
In an action for relief against a voidable transfer or obligation, and subject to the statute's protections for good-faith transferees, the statute lets a creditor obtain: avoidance of the transfer or obligation to the extent necessary to satisfy the creditor's claim; an attachment or other provisional remedy against the transferred asset or other property of the transferee, following the attachment procedures in the Code of Civil Procedure or other applicable law; and, subject to equitable principles and applicable procedural rules, an injunction against further disposition of the transferred asset or other property of the transferee by the debtor or transferee, appointment of a receiver to take charge of the transferred asset or other such property, or any other relief the circumstances may require. In addition, if the creditor has already obtained a judgment against the debtor, the creditor may levy execution on the transferred asset or its proceeds.

This clause does not evaluate whether any of these factors is present with respect to any specific transfer involving any particular debtor, and satisfying one or more of these factors does not, by itself, establish actual intent to hinder, delay, or defraud under the statute.

expectedJSON.body: Separate from actual intent, the statute lets a creditor void a transfer or obligation based purely on the debtor's objective financial circumstances, with no need to prove the debtor's state of mind. One provision, available to any creditor regardless of whether the creditor's claim arose before or after the transfer, makes a transfer or obligation voidable if the debtor did not receive a reasonably equivalent value in exchange, and the debtor either was engaged in or about to engage in a business or transaction for which the debtor's remaining assets were unreasonably small in relation to that business or transaction, or intended to incur, or believed or reasonably should have believed the debtor would incur, debts beyond the debtor's ability to pay them as they became due. A second, narrower provision applies only to a creditor whose claim arose before the transfer was made or the obligation was incurred: it makes the transfer or obligation voidable if the debtor did not receive a reasonably equivalent value in exchange and the debtor either was already insolvent at that time or became insolvent as a result of the transfer or obligation. In both provisions, the creditor bears the burden of proving the elements of the claim for relief by a preponderance of the evidence.

citations.cite: Uniform Voidable Transactions Act, constructive fraud available to any creditor
citations.quote: Without receiving a reasonably equivalent value in exchange for the transfer or obligation, and the debtor either:(A) Was engaged or was about to engage in a business or a transaction for which the remaining assets of the debtor were unreasonably small in relation to the business or transaction.(B) Intended to incur, or believed or reasonably should have believed that the debtor would incur, debts beyond the debtor’s ability to pay as they became due.

citations.cite: Uniform Voidable Transactions Act, constructive fraud limited to pre-existing creditors
citations.quote: A transfer made or obligation incurred by a debtor is voidable as to a creditor whose claim arose before the transfer was made or the obligation was incurred if the debtor made the transfer or incurred the obligation without receiving a reasonably equivalent value in exchange for the transfer or obligation and the debtor was insolvent at that time or the debtor became insolvent as a result of the transfer or obligation.

expectedJSON.gap: This clause covers two distinct statutory provisions with different creditor eligibility: Civil Code section 3439.04(a)(2), open to any creditor regardless of when the claim arose and keyed to unreasonably small remaining assets or an intent/belief about future ability to pay debts; and Civil Code section 3439.05, limited to creditors whose claim predates the transfer and keyed to actual insolvency rather than merely a risk of it. The research brief that framed this document described these as a single combined test (no reasonably equivalent value plus insolvency, unreasonably small assets, or intent to incur debts beyond ability to pay, treated as three interchangeable alternatives); the statute as actually codified instead splits these into two separate provisions with different creditor scope, which this clause corrects and states separately rather than merging. This clause does not determine whether any specific debtor received reasonably equivalent value for, or was insolvent or undercapitalized at the time of, any specific transfer.

expectedJSON.body: The statute extinguishes a cause of action under the Uniform Voidable Transactions Act unless the creditor brings an action, or makes a levy, within specific time limits, and those limits differ by which ground for voidability is invoked. For an actual-intent claim, the action must be brought no later than four years after the transfer was made or the obligation was incurred, or, if later, no later than one year after the transfer or obligation was or reasonably could have been discovered by the claimant. For either constructive-fraud claim, the action must be brought no later than four years after the transfer was made or the obligation was incurred, with no discovery-based extension. Separately, and regardless of which of these grounds applies or when the transfer or obligation was or could have been discovered, the statute imposes an absolute seven-year outer limit: a cause of action under the statute is extinguished if no action is brought and no levy is made within seven years after the transfer was made or the obligation was incurred, notwithstanding any other provision of law.

citations.cite: Uniform Voidable Transactions Act, limitations period for actual-intent claims
citations.quote: Under paragraph (1) of subdivision (a) of Section 3439.04, not later than four years after the transfer was made or the obligation was incurred or, if later, not later than one year after the transfer or obligation was or could reasonably have been discovered by the claimant.

citations.cite: Uniform Voidable Transactions Act, limitations period for constructive-fraud claims
citations.quote: Under paragraph (2) of subdivision (a) of Section 3439.04 or Section 3439.05, not later than four years after the transfer was made or the obligation was incurred.

citations.cite: Uniform Voidable Transactions Act, seven-year outer repose period
citations.quote: Notwithstanding any other provision of law, a cause of action under this chapter with respect to a transfer or obligation is extinguished if no action is brought or levy made within seven years after the transfer was made or the obligation was incurred.

expectedJSON.gap: This clause quotes Civil Code section 3439.09(a), (b), and (c) in full; the research brief that framed this document referred generally to a single "statute of limitations/repose period," but the statute as actually codified sets three different time rules — a four-year-or-one-year-discovery period for actual-intent claims, a flat four-year period for constructive-fraud claims, and a seven-year absolute repose period that overrides both — which this clause states separately rather than as one period. This clause does not calculate any specific deadline for any particular debtor or creditor and does not address how a court would determine when a transfer or obligation "was or could reasonably have been discovered" on any particular set of facts.

expectedJSON.body: In an action for relief against a voidable transfer or obligation, and subject to the statute's protections for good-faith transferees, the statute lets a creditor obtain: avoidance of the transfer or obligation to the extent necessary to satisfy the creditor's claim; an attachment or other provisional remedy against the transferred asset or other property of the transferee, following the attachment procedures in the Code of Civil Procedure or other applicable law; and, subject to equitable principles and applicable procedural rules, an injunction against further disposition of the transferred asset or other property of the transferee by the debtor or transferee, appointment of a receiver to take charge of the transferred asset or other such property, or any other relief the circumstances may require. In addition, if the creditor has already obtained a judgment against the debtor, the creditor may levy execution on the transferred asset or its proceeds.

citations.cite: Uniform Voidable Transactions Act, remedies in an action for relief
citations.quote: In an action for relief against a transfer or obligation under this chapter, a creditor, subject to the limitations in Section 3439.08, may obtain:(1) Avoidance of the transfer or obligation to the extent necessary to satisfy the creditor’s claim.(2) An attachment or other provisional remedy against the asset transferred or other property of the transferee in accordance with the procedures described in Title 6.5 (commencing with Section 481.010) of Part 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure, or as may otherwise be available under applicable law.(3) Subject to applicable principles of equity and in accordance with applicable rules of civil procedure, the following:(A) An injunction against further disposition by the debtor or a transferee, or both, of the asset transferred or other property of the transferee.(B) Appointment of a receiver to take charge of the asset transferred or other property of the transferee.(C) Any other relief the circumstances may require.

citations.cite: Uniform Voidable Transactions Act, levy of execution after judgment
citations.quote: If a creditor has obtained a judgment on a claim against the debtor, the creditor may levy execution on the asset transferred or its proceeds.

expectedJSON.gap: This clause quotes Civil Code section 3439.07(a) and (c); it does not restate subdivision (b) of the same section (attachment while an action on the underlying claim is pending, before judgment) or subdivision (d) (rights of an assignee for the benefit of creditors), and it does not address the separate rules in Civil Code section 3439.08 that limit or qualify these remedies against a good-faith transferee for value, which the quoted text expressly cross-references but which this clause does not independently detail. This clause does not determine what specific remedy, if any, a court would grant to any particular creditor against any particular debtor on any particular transfer.
